cards.explanation: The answer is His power. Asaph says, "They did not remember His power…" and the verse goes right on to the day He redeemed them from the adversary (Psalm 78:42). I lose my oven mitts three times a week, so I get forgetting small things, friends. But forgetting a rescue like that? That's a big one to let slip.

The answer is False. The verse says He turned their rivers to blood, "…and from their streams they could not drink" (Psalm 78:44). The very streams the Egyptians counted on were off the table for drinking. If my water did that, I'd close the bakery for the day and sit down.

The answer is their vines and their cattle. Asaph says, "He killed their vines with hailstones and their sycamore-figs with sleet." Then He "…abandoned their cattle to the hail and their livestock to bolts of lightning" (Psalm 78:47-48). Fields and herds both got hit, friends, and the weather did the work.

The answer is like sheep in a flock. Asaph says, "He led out His people like sheep and guided them like a flock in the wilderness" (Psalm 78:52). I love the picture, friends. A flock follows its shepherd, and the shepherd does the leading.

The answer is True. Asaph says, "He led them safely, so they did not fear…" (Psalm 78:53). Safe, so no fear. I get jumpy on a stepladder, so I'm impressed. Their safety came from the One leading them.

The answer is that the sea engulfed them. Asaph says, "…but the sea engulfed their enemies" (Psalm 78:53). God's people went through safely and the enemies did not. It's the same sea Asaph sang about earlier in this psalm, when God split it (Psalm 78:13).

The answer is inheritance. Asaph says God "…drove out nations before them and apportioned their inheritance; He settled the tribes of Israel in their tents" (Psalm 78:55). Apportioned means divided up. Picture a big pan of cookies cut so every tribe gets a piece, friends.

The answer is True. Asaph says, "They turned back and were faithless like their fathers, twisted like a faulty bow" (Psalm 78:57). That echoes the start of this psalm, where he hoped the children wouldn't be stubborn like their fathers (Psalm 78:8). I think that's why this line stings.

The answer is idols. Asaph says, "They enraged Him with their high places and provoked His jealousy with their idols" (Psalm 78:58). High places and idols are the two things he names in this verse, friends. Both of them stirred up God's anger.

The answer is the tabernacle of Shiloh. Asaph says, "He abandoned the tabernacle of Shiloh, the tent He had pitched among men" (Psalm 78:60). A tabernacle is a tent, and he says God had pitched it among men. It's a heavy line, friends, so I'll let it sit.

The answer is shame. Asaph says, "He beat back His foes; He put them to everlasting shame" (Psalm 78:66). The foes get beaten back, and the shame he names is everlasting. After the heavy verses before it, this is where things turn, friends.

The answer is False. After rejecting Joseph's tent and Ephraim, Asaph says, "But He chose the tribe of Judah, Mount Zion, which He loved" (Psalm 78:67-68). That "But" is doing a lot of work in the verse. God chose Judah.

The answer is False. Asaph says, "He built His sanctuary like the heights, like the earth He has established forever" (Psalm 78:69). My cookie planet is just big enough for a bakery, so a comparison to the whole earth impresses me. He picks the heights and the earth, friends, not a tent.

The answer is shepherd of His people. Asaph says, "…from tending the ewes He brought him to be shepherd of His people Jacob, of Israel His inheritance" (Psalm 78:70-71). David went from tending the ewes to shepherding God's people. The word shepherd stays, friends, and the ones he looks after change.

The answer is with integrity of heart. Asaph says, "So David shepherded them with integrity of heart and guided them with skillful hands" (Psalm 78:72). The heart and the hands both get named, bakers. That's a lovely way to end a long song.
